At the end of 2008, Resolution 1850 declared the Council's support for the Israeli-Palestinian peace talks restarted at Annapolis. It was a rare Middle East text that the United States helped draft and all members backed. The members called the negotiations irreversible.

Inside, the text backs the two-state goal, praises both sides' commitments, and urges donors to fund the Palestinian Authority. It also calls on regional states to support the process and cut ties with violence. Adopted days before the Gaza war began, it preserves the last shared statement of a peace effort about to collapse.
plos-pone-0000050:
Karla Eger, Mark Sundrud, Alison Motsinger, and co-authors showed in 2006 that one class of immune cells is far from uniform. Natural killer T cells patrol for abnormal cells and can release signals that steer the whole immune response. A key question was whether they can reprogram those effector functions, switching the kind of signal they send.

The team found human natural killer T cells are heterogeneous in that capacity: some can reprogram, others are more fixed. A mixed population changes how doctors should think about using these cells in therapy, since the helpful subset may need to be picked out. The study maps variety where earlier work had assumed sameness.
gregory-great-morals-on-job-vol-3-part-1:
The first half of volume three of Gregory the Great's Morals on the Book of Job came out in 1850, in the Rev. James Bliss translation. The Moralia, written in the late 500s, is Gregory's verse-by-verse reading of Job and the largest work he ever produced. This part opens the final stretch of that reading.

Gregory is now deep into Job's long speeches and God's reply from the storm. His method stays the same: history first, then the teaching hidden in the words, then the moral for daily life. He lingers on pride, hidden sin, and the limits of human judgment. The volume carries the commentary toward its close in the following part.
gregory-great-morals-on-job-vol-3-part-2:
Volume three, part two of Gregory the Great's Morals on the Book of Job, published in 1850, closes the Rev. James Bliss English translation. It covers Books Thirty through Thirty-five of the Moralia, the commentary Gregory wrote in the late 500s, and it adds the indexes for the whole set.

In these last books Gregory works through the end of Job: the great speeches on God's power in nature, Job's humble reply, and his restoration. Leviathan and Behemoth become figures for evil and pride. Gregory sums up his lifelong theme, that suffering rightly borne purges the soul. The ending completes the most widely read Bible commentary of the early Middle Ages.

frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d350:
Steve Early, the President's secretary, telegraphed Harry Hopkins from Washington on 2 December 1943 with the American reaction to the Cairo communiqué. Sent by military channels, the message mixes celebration at the statement's reception with anger at how its secrecy was broken.

The communiqué, Early reports, was received with enthusiasm across the country, with great praise and jubilation in all quarters. That came despite Reuters' Lisbon dispatch. The dispatch printed virtually the whole Cairo story almost twenty-four hours before the release. It cut the statement's force. It also let German and Japanese propagandists broadcast their versions in the gap. Early urges shorter intervals between distribution and publication for any future communiqués, and a strict ban on sending their contents abroad before the release date.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d450: Document 450 is a short piece of editorial writing, not a 1943 dispatch. Historians in the Office of the Historian prepared notes like it for the Cairo-Tehran volume. They use the notes to add context the wartime papers lack. Sometimes they point to documents printed elsewhere in the series. The conferences covered here shaped Allied plans for 1944 and beyond. keyhoe-flying-saucers-are-real-1950:

atwood-suggestive-inquiry-1850:

hermes-pymander-everard-1650:

dickens-david-copperfield-1850:

dumas-black-tulip-1850:

hawthorne-scarlet-letter-1850:
Nathaniel Hawthorne published The Scarlet Letter in 1850, his great novel of guilt and Puritan conscience. emerson-representative-men-1850:

Emerson treats each man as the lens of an age, great because he sees for all. Plato stands for philosophy, Shakespeare for poetry, and Napoleon for the power of common will in action. baxter-saints-everlasting-rest-1650:

Baxter paints heaven as rest after labor, reunion with the saints, and unbroken sight of God. He scolds cold hearts and gives practical rules for pondering eternal things amid business and pain. hohman-long-lost-friend-1850:

Its short entries tell how to stop bleeding, cure burns, break fevers, protect cattle, and guard a house from fire and thieves. Most cures join a spoken charm in the name of the Trinity to a small rite or herb. Families kept the book in kitchens and barns for everyday emergencies.
sendivogius-new-light-of-alchymie-1650:

He teaches that a hidden food of life, drawn from the air and the sun's rays, feeds metals growing in the earth. The philosophers' stone, in his account, concentrates that food until base metals ripen into gold. His clear, confident system made him the most readable of the great alchemical teachers. His name for that hidden food, the seed of nature, passed into wide use.
calmet-phantom-world-1850:

Calmet studied reports of apparitions, vampires, and corpses that seemed to return from the grave. His work first appeared in the 1740s and drew wide debate.

Calmet weighed church teaching, witness reports, and tales from eastern Europe, where vampire panics were recent news. He asked whether such returns were real, fraud, disease, or error, and he did not settle every case. His careful, doubting tone made the book a key early study of ghosts and vampires, quoted by later writers for two centuries.
bastiat-the-law-1850:

Bastiat, an economist and member of France's assembly, defended natural law against what he called legal plunder. The pamphlet became the classic statement of classical-liberal legal philosophy in miniature.

Law, Bastiat argued, exists only to defend life, liberty, and property, the gifts that come before law itself. When law takes from some to give to others, it perverts its purpose and teaches theft. He wrote with wit and plain examples drawn from French politics of his day. The Law fits in an hour's reading, yet its phrases are still quoted wherever state power is debated.
sydenham-works-vol2-1850:

Here Sydenham treats smallpox, gout, and several other common diseases of his day. He explains the cooling treatment he used for smallpox and describes his own painful attacks of gout. Throughout, he trusts what repeated observation shows over what old books claim. The volume rounds out the record of his clinical method, and it shows why later doctors admired his honest, practical style.
tennyson-in-memoriam-1850:

He published the gathered sequence, 131 lyrics with prologue and epilogue, as In Memoriam in 1850, without his name at first.

wordsworth-prelude-1850:

turgenev-diary-superfluous-man-garnett-1:

braid-observations-on-trance-1850:

dods-philosophy-electrical-psychology-18:

bonatti-de-astronomia-tractatus-1550:

Theta's memory-making power, counted, exploratory conduct's neural mark, dentate gyrus excitability cycling, synaptic weights modified rhythmically, spatial encoding's rhythmic basis.
plos-pone-0006450: Beeps can fake extra flashes. Innes-Brown and Crewther found spatial gaps weaken the sound-induced flash illusion. Ears fool eyes, but distance breaks the spell — senses crossing wires, mapped, where one flash meets two beeps. Delay kills it too: space now tested.
plos-pone-0006550: Blind-sight fish think they move. Huang and team found belladonna zebrafish feel false self-motion from crossed eye wiring. The mutant's vision lies — fish fooled by their own eyes, tested, with an lhx2 gene hit. Optic nerves not crossed, no chiasm formed.
plos-pone-0009450: Flu is usually a winter story, but in warm regions it marches to a different drum. This paper builds a model linking weather data — humidity, temperature — to flu spread in tropical and subtropical areas. The results help health officials in warm climates predict when flu will surge, so vaccines and hospital beds arrive before the wave, not after.
plos-pone-0009550: Comparing millions of protein sequences is slow with traditional alignment. This paper proposes a shortcut: convert each sequence into a feature vector of its building-block counts and positions, then compare vectors. The method trades a little precision for a lot of speed — a practical tool for the age of big biological data.
plos-pone-0009650: Grey reef sharks roam the Indo-Pacific, but how far do individuals travel — and do they stay loyal to one reef? This tracking study maps large-scale movements and reef fidelity. The paper reveals the travel habits of a top reef predator, informing marine protection.
plos-pone-0010450: In meningitis, Listeria germs meet the brain's hair-lined walls. This study grows the two together and watches both sides shift their habits. The lab meeting shows how brain infection digs in at the organ's gates. The findings hint at new ways to block the germ's foothold.
plos-pone-0010550: Growing kidneys in a dish needs the right conditions. This study presents a low-volume culture method that preserves cortico-medullary organization. The paper improves a key tool for studying kidney development. The advance lets researchers watch kidneys build themselves.
plos-pone-0010650: Lyme disease comes in many Borrelia flavors. This study surveys genotypic variation in ticks across North America and Europe. The paper maps the diversity behind a spreading disease. The diversity map aids diagnosis and tick tracking across two continents and oceans.
plos-pone-0010750: Gaucher disease leaves the body short of a key enzyme. This mouse study pits two enzyme-replacement drugs against each other to see if they match. The paper tests whether the two work the same. The results guide care for this rare inherited illness.
plos-pone-0010850: Germs may do more than inflame tissue — they may arm tumors. This study shows bits of bacterial wall make breast cancer cells more invasive through the TLR2 sensor. The paper links bugs to spread. The sensor becomes a treatment target. The finding reframes infection as a cancer ally.
plos-pone-0010950: Millennium Atoll may be the most pristine reef left. This study surveyed its lagoon's nature during a 2009 expedition to Kiribati. The paper records a baseline paradise. The data anchor Pacific conservation. The baseline is a precious gift to future scientists.
plos-pone-0011050: Recognizing faces may not depend on where your eyes dart. This eye-tracking and brain-imaging study finds scanning strategies don't change face-identification performance. The paper separates seeing from processing. The finding refines models of visual cognition. The separation clarifies how faces are read.
plos-pone-0011150: Dementia patients who can't consent still join research. This Italian study asks how legislation protects the interests of incapacitated research participants. The paper reviews legal agency for dementia patients. The finding informs research ethics. The ethics balance science with dignity.
plos-pone-0011250: 'Natural' on the label may not mean greener. This soybean study finds organic pesticides can harm the environment as much as man-made ones. The paper busts a green myth. The finding aids farm policy. The farm lesson: judge sprays by data.
plos-pone-0011350: Brain cells ship RNA notes in protein parcels. This study maps the protein makeup of Staufen2 parcels in young rat brains. The paper reveals a delivery crew. The finding aids brain science. The aided science maps RNA delivery. The mapped delivery explains brain growth.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1250:
The White House Map Room wrote to Ambassador Hurley in China on 25 July 1945. The Map Room was the president's own message center, the small staff that handled his secret traffic with posts and commanders around the world. Its cables spoke with his authority.

A Map Room message to an envoy carried the president's word without the forms of a department letter. Hurley in China received it as direct guidance from the top. This note shows that swift, private channel at work during the summit. It linked the president's traveling court to a distant post in a single step.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1350:
J. Rives Childs, the American representative in the talks about Tangier, reported to the acting secretary of state on 18 July 1945. Tangier, the port city at the mouth of the Mediterranean, had a special status shared by several powers. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Tangier was a small place with an outsized diplomatic file, since its rule had been shared before the war and seized by Spain during it. Childs took part in the talks meant to settle the city's future. His report shows a side negotiation running beside the Potsdam summit. Such quiet work filled most of the department's days, even in historic weeks.
frus-1945-50-intel-d50:
Minutes of the 170th meeting of the Secretary of State's Staff Committee are dated 27 November 1945. Two numbered meetings within a week point to a heavy agenda at the department. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

The staff committee was Secretary Byrnes's inner council on department business. Its minutes for late November belong to the weeks when the intelligence plans of State, War. The Budget Bureau were being forced into one shape. Readers should note the pace: the 168th meeting on the 20th, the 170th on the 27th. Institutions meet this often when a decision is near and the details will not settle themselves.
frus-1945-50-intel-d150:
On 9 May 1946, the President’s Chief of Staff (Leahy) sent a memorandum to President Truman. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 150 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The postwar system was still new: the National Intelligence Authority gave the orders, and the Central Intelligence Group carried them out.

The memo form let a staff officer speak straight to a chief: here is the point, here are the facts, here is what is asked. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1945-50-intel-d250:
A text titled "Memorandum of Discussion at the 2d Meeting of the National Security Council" bears the date 14 November 1947. It stands as document 250 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. By law the CIA now stood where the Central Intelligence Group had stood, and the National Security Council sat above it.

Where no stenographer sat in, a memcon is the meeting. It holds the talk in the words of the man who wrote it up. So the talk could guide later work, each point is set down while its weight is still clear. The Council was still new, and its early meetings worked out how the president's top advisers would handle defense and foreign policy together.
frus-1945-50-intel-d350:
A memorandum from Robert G. Barnes reached William J. McWilliams of the Executive Secretariat on 25 August 1948. The State Department prints it as document 350 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. It was a season of stock-taking: the CIA was a year old, and its friends and critics were both writing things down.

Such notes moved business along: they told a busy reader what had happened, what it meant, and what should come next. Whole policies can be traced through chains of such notes, each one moving the matter a step. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1861-d50:
Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 7 June 1861. The dispatch is document 50 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Adams wrote in a spare, exact style that Seward learned to trust. His June reports cover talks, notes, and the mood of the British press. For readers, they are a model of how a skilled envoy turns daily talk into clear word for his chief. Seward read Adams's reports with close care and often shared them with the cabinet. Cabinet eyes on his pages made Adams the best read envoy of the war.
frus-1861-d150:
A letter of 5 September 1861 went from William H. Seward to William Dayton in Paris. The letter is document 150 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

September letters from Seward turn to trade, ships, and the fine print of neutrality. The grand pleas of spring gave way to detail. This note to Paris shows high policy becoming clerk's work, which is where it was won or lost. Detail, Seward knew, was where neutral pledges were kept or quietly broken. Neutral pledges live or die in details, and Seward never forgot that truth. Fine print was where pledges lived or died.
frus-1861-d250:
Writing on 4 September 1861, James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands sent his report to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It was printed as Document 250 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. The date falls in the first summer of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d50:
Seward wrote again on 19 April 1862, this time to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It was printed as Document 50 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. It belongs to the spring of 1862, a year into the war, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d150:
Circular No. 24, dated 25 September 1862, is Document 150 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. A circular was not a private letter but a single set of orders sent at the same time to many American envoys and consuls abroad. So that all of them spoke with one voice.

Seward used circulars when Washington needed the same line taken in every capital at once. This one went out three days after Lincoln announced his emancipation plan, in a week when foreign governments were reassessing the war. It shows the State Department managing its whole foreign service as one body, not post by post.
frus-1862-d250:
William L. Dayton reported from Paris on 21 January 1862 in a letter printed as Document 250 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It went to Secretary of State William H. Seward, though it stands in the file after a later Seward letter.

The printers grouped some papers out of date order, so this report follows the dispatch it may have crossed at sea. Dayton's mail gave Washington its best read on Napoleon III's court, where policy could shift with one man's mood. Reports from his hand shaped how the Union handled France all year. The Paris mail sailed from Le Havre and took about two weeks to reach Washington.
frus-1862-d350:
Henri Mercier, the French minister in Washington, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 23 December 1861, in a letter printed as Document 350 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Mercier wrote two days before Washington settled the Trent affair by freeing the seized envoys. French diplomacy had counseled calm in that crisis, which Washington noted with gratitude. His letter belongs to the closing days of the year's worst foreign scare, when the French channel proved one of the steadiest Seward had. The French legation's notes were written in French and printed here in the Department's English. Cases in this channel often mixed the war at home with French designs in Mexico.
frus-1862-d450:
John Lothrop Motley, the American minister in Vienna, received this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 10 January 1862. It is Document 450 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, opening the Austrian file.

Motley was already famous as the historian of the Dutch republic when Lincoln sent him to Austria. Vienna was a conservative court, cool toward republics, and its view of the American war was shaped by its fear of revolution at home. Seward's opening order for the year armed Motley with the Union's case. The dispatch begins a file written by one of the most literary men ever to hold an American post abroad.
frus-1862-d550:
A second note of 30 September 1862 went from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Roest van Limburg. It stands as Document 550 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, beside its same-day companion.

Paired notes on one day meant separate subjects, each answered in its own letter under the Department's standing practice. The Dutch file had run that way since June, and the habit gives the modern reader a clean record: no mixed paragraphs, no buried answers. Van Limburg's government got from Seward that day two distinct statements it could file and quote. The pair closes the September Dutch exchange, one of the most orderly in a volume full of harder and hotter correspondence.
frus-1862-d650:
Dated 17 May 1862, this dispatch from Robert H. Pruyn reached Secretary of State William H. Seward as part of the regular mail from Japan. Pruyn was the American minister there, in the first weeks of his time in the post. The letter is document 650 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Note the dates around it: Pruyn wrote again and again that May, a sign of how much a new envoy had to report. His letters told Washington about the legation's talks and troubles in a land the United States had known for less than a decade. Each one adds a page to that early record.
frus-1863p1-d50: This untitled paper is dated 25 October 1862 and printed as document 50 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It sits inside the group of Confederate letters in that part, between papers of Mallory and Memminger. The evidence gives its date and place in the run, but no title, writer, or name addressed.
frus-1863p1-d150:
On 9 April 1863, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward for the second time that day. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 150 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, carrying a round number in the count.

The middle sheet of Adams's 9 April set holds its own head of the brief, as his sets always did. That spring the heads were ships and the law that might hold them. This letter is the second of the three. With its mates, it rounds out a day on which the London post worked the full width of the Union's case in Britain.
frus-1863p1-d250: Document 250 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume is an untitled paper dated 28 July 1863. It sits inside the long run of letters between Secretary of State William H. Seward and Charles Francis Adams in London, the channel that handled relations with Britain during the Civil War. The catalog gives it no title or author, so its place in that correspondence is what the record shows.
frus-1863p1-d350: On 3 January 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 350 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, part of the formal exchange through which the two governments handled Civil War disputes. Notes on this route dealt with neutral rights, stopped ships, and British complaints.
frus-1863p1-d450:
William H. Seward, Secretary of State took up his pen on 7 April 1863 and wrote to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail.

A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d550:
William H. Seward took up his pen on 5 June 1863 and wrote to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d650:
On 29 October 1863, the American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams in London was the Union's front line in Britain, pressing its case with the British government week after week. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the autumn of 1863.

Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
plos-pbio-0020050:
Haoxing Xu, Jie Jin, Louis J. DeFelice, and their team reported a surprise about metal transport in PLOS Biology in 2004. A protein called DMT1 is the main route for iron to enter mammalian cells. A mutation that keeps turning up in the protein revealed something extra: a path for calcium entry.

Mutations that appear again and again often mark a spot a protein cannot do without. Here, studying that spot exposed a hidden side of DMT1's work. The finding widens the picture of how cells handle metals, where iron and calcium traffic may cross. It may also help explain odd symptoms in people and animals with faults in this transporter.
plos-pone-0000150:
Roman H. Khonsari and Vincent Calvez published this theory paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It addresses concentric demyelination, a striking pattern seen in some brain lesions where myelin, the insulation around nerve fibers, is lost in rings. The authors model how such rings could arise through self-organization in the human brain.

Ring-shaped damage is hard to explain by simple spreading. A self-organization model shows how local interactions can build the pattern without a ring-shaped cause. The work offers neurologists a new way to think about an unusual lesion pattern. It also shows how maths can suggest mechanisms for diseases that are hard to study directly.
plos-pone-0000250:
Sagi Levy, Jan Ihmels, Miri Carmi, and colleagues published this yeast genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Budding yeast is a single-celled fungus and a workhorse of genetics. The authors lay out the strategy of transcription regulation in this yeast. It is the overall logic by which the yeast decides which genes to switch on and when.

A strategy-level view shows design principles: how one regulator can serve many conditions, and how the system stays flexible. The authors draw that logic from genome-wide data. Understanding yeast regulation guides work in more complex cells, where the same principles apply with more parts.
plos-pone-0000350:
Gianfranco Diretto, Salim Al-Babili, Raffaela Tavazza, and colleagues published this plant engineering paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Carotenoids are the pigments that make carrots orange and supply vitamin A. The authors use metabolic engineering to raise potato carotenoid content, switching on a bacterial mini-pathway only in the tuber, the part people eat.

Potatoes are a staple for millions, so enriching them could fight vitamin A deficiency at scale. A tuber-specific pathway avoids burdening the rest of the plant. The paper reports the engineered potatoes' carotenoid gains, a step in the biofortification program for staple crops.
plos-pone-0000450:
Hu-Hui Lee and Richard R. Behringer switched a developmental gene on during cartilage formation and watched the result, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The gene is Wnt4, a signal that guides building in the embryo. Using conditional expression, a method that turns the gene on only in chosen tissue and time, they activated it during chondrogenesis in mice.

The outcome was dwarfism: the mice grew up short-limbed. Cartilage is the template that bone later replaces, so a signal that disturbs cartilage growth reshapes the whole skeleton. The experiment shows Wnt4's dose and timing must be tightly controlled for normal bone length, a lesson relevant to human skeletal disorders.
plos-pone-0000550:
A. D. McNaghten and colleagues argued for a fairer way to watch the HIV epidemic in the United States, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Existing behavioral and clinical surveillance drew on convenience samples that may not represent all persons with HIV. The authors set out the rationale for developing a population-based approach to improve representativeness.

If surveillance misses whole groups, programs aim at the wrong targets and disparities stay hidden. A population-based design samples so that every group counts in proportion. Methods papers like this one do quiet but durable work: they change the data every later decision depends on.
plos-pone-0000650:
Mike M. Moradian, Denis Beglaryan, Jill M. Skozylas and colleagues sequenced the full mitochondrial genomes of three Tetrahymena species for PLOS ONE in 2007. Tetrahymena is a single-celled ciliate used widely as a model organism. Its mitochondrial genome is divergent and unusual. Half of its 44 genes still lacked a definite function.

Those genes fall into known protein-coding genes and a group called Ymf genes. The title reports mutation hot spots and faster nonsynonymous change in the Ymf group. Nonsynonymous changes alter the protein a gene encodes, so their speed says something about evolutionary pressure. Comparative sequences like these help untangle how this odd genome evolved.
plos-pone-0000750:
Delphine Hu, Stefano M. Bertozzi, Emmanuela Gakidou and colleagues weighed what it costs to keep mothers alive in Mexico. Writing in PLOS ONE in 2007, they give Mexico's lifetime risk of dying from maternal causes as 1 in 370. The United States figure was 1 in 2,500. National efforts had improved maternal services over the prior decade, but progress toward Millennium Development Goal 5 was unclear.

The team assessed costs, benefits, and cost-effectiveness of interventions against maternal illness and death. Money spent on the wrong mix of services saves fewer mothers. Their accounting gives policymakers a ranked case for where the next peso does the most good.
plos-pone-0000850:
Allan Saul and Michael P. Fay analyzed how human immunity should shape vaccines that bundle several components against one target. Including multiple immunogens against one organism is a strategy pursued for many trial vaccines. It helps most where one immunogen alone cannot raise a strongly protective response. Many existing human vaccines already contain multiple components.

Their 2007 PLOS ONE question is design logic: given how human immunity actually responds, when do extra components help, and when do they compete? Immune responses can focus on a few dominant targets, wasting the rest. Sound design rules save vaccine developers from bloated formulas, and they matter most for hard targets like malaria and HIV.
plos-pone-0000950:
Marco Salemi, Brant Burkhardt, Rebecca Gray and colleagues traced how HIV changes inside different tissues, in PLOS ONE in 2007. As HIV infection advances, the virus often switches which cell door it uses, from CCR5 to CXCR4. The CXCR4 forms are especially deadly to young thymus cells.

Almost no work had checked which virus forms live inside the thymus itself. The team compare viral populations in lymphoid and other tissues. Their analysis gives the thymus a central role in the emergence of the CXCR4 forms. That finding ties a turning point in disease to one small organ where T cells mature.
plos-pone-0001050:
Yulei Wang, Catalin Barbacioru, Dov Shiffman and colleagues found a blood gene signature for a hidden artery swelling, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Thoracic aortic aneurysm is a bulge in the main artery near the heart. It usually gives no symptoms, yet it kills at high rates when it bursts. Surgery can prevent that, but finding who is at risk is hard.

The team hypothesized that gene expression patterns in peripheral blood could betray the aneurysm. A blood test for a silent, deadly swelling would change screening entirely. Their signature work is a first step: show the signal exists in an easy sample before building a clinic ready test.
plos-pone-0001150:
When a broken bone heals, the body rebuilds it using two routes: one that first lays down cartilage, and one that forms bone directly. Danielle Behonick and colleagues examined an enzyme's part in both routes, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The enzyme is matrix metalloproteinase 13, also called collagenase-3, which cuts collagen.

The enzyme was already known to matter in long bone development. The authors found it is expressed during adult skeletal repair and tested its role in regeneration after injury. Their work links the reshaping of the matrix around cells to successful bone healing in adults.
plos-pone-0001250:
The brain rewires itself as it adapts, but how its own activity changes the strength of its connections is largely unknown. Masako Tsukamoto-Yasui and colleagues report observations from the hippocampus, a region central to memory, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They describe active hippocampal networks undergoing spontaneous synaptic modification.

In their experiments, synapses changed strength without an external lesson driving them, following the network's own activity. The brain, in their phrase, is self-writable. Findings like these bear on how memories form and how networks stay stable while remaining flexible.
plos-pone-0001350:
Thousands of systematic reviews summarize health care evidence. Such reviews sit near the top of the evidence ladder in medicine. But their quality varies, and it should routinely be appraised. Beverley Shea and colleagues externally validated AMSTAR, a measurement tool for assessing systematic reviews, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They used the tool to appraise 42 reviews.

External validation asks whether a tool works in hands other than its makers'. AMSTAR has since become a standard checklist for review quality. The paper helped establish whether its scores are reliable and meaningful for judging the reviews on which clinical guidelines rest.
plos-pone-0001450:
Zhuofei Xu and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study that reads the full genome of a pig germ. The germ causes a lung ill in pigs that costs farms a great deal world wide. The strain they read is a type common in China. Its full gene code gives a base for all later work on this germ.

The full code lets labs compare this strain with kin strains from other lands, gene by gene. That base lets them spot vaccine and drug targets with far more care than before. It also lets vets track how strains spread and change. That is key for a disease that moves with the pig trade.
plos-pone-0001550:
Joseph Lemire, Ryan Mailloux, and Vasu Appanna wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on lactate use in human brain tumor cells. Lactate was long seen as a waste end of energy work without air. Its fate in brain chemistry was not pinned down. The team tested a human astrocytoma cell line, a model of a common brain tumor cell.

They show, for the first time in this line, that the cells can take in and burn lactate for energy. An enzyme inside the cell power units drives that use. The result recasts lactate as a fuel, not just waste. It may shape how brain tumors are fed and fought.
plos-pone-0001650:
Mikhail M. Pooggin, Johannes Fütterer, and Thomas Hohn compared a protein-making trick used by two plant viruses in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Cauliflower mosaic virus infects broad-leaf plants, while rice tungro bacilliform virus infects rice. Both are pararetroviruses, and both pack several genes onto one RNA strand. To read the later genes, ribosomes shunt: they start, then jump past a section to the next start point.

The authors asked whether the shunt parts from one virus work in the other, across the wide gap between the plant groups they infect. The full text gives the swap tests and how much protein each version made. Shared function across such different viruses hints that this jump mechanism is old and sturdy. It also gives plant science a tested tool for making several proteins from one gene strand.
plos-pone-0001750:
Henry Haeberle, Leigh A. Bryan, Tegy J. Vadakkan, and their co-authors studied touch sensor cells in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Merkel cell-neurite complexes are among the most sensitive touch receptors in skin, pairing epidermal Merkel cells with sensory nerve endings. Merkel cells are proposed to be the sensing cells that signal nerves chemically, but functional proof was thin.

The team reports that swelling-activated calcium channels trigger calcium signals in Merkel cells. Calcium signals are how such cells would pass the touch message onward. The full text gives the cell recordings and channel tests. Pinning a channel to the first step of touch helps explain fine fingertip sensitivity and may guide work on touch loss.
plos-pone-0001850:
Anandharaman Veerapathran, Rajnish Joshi, Kalyan Goswami, and their co-authors set cut-off values for tuberculosis blood tests in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Blood tests called IGRAs are a promising alternative to the tuberculin skin test. Reading repeated tests is hampered by lack of evidence on the best cut-offs for flips. A flip is the point where a result counts as newly positive or back to negative.

Using repeat testing data, the team derived cut-offs from how much one person's T-cell assay results vary. The full text gives the spread of results and the proposed thresholds. Health workers screened again and again, such as hospital staff, need such thresholds to avoid chasing noise as if it were new infection.
plos-pone-0001950:
Caroline Charlier and co-authors matched brain scans to illness severity in a fungal brain infection, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The infection, cryptococcal meningoencephalitis, strikes people with HIV and kills about one in five despite antifungal drugs. Doctors lacked a sharp way to grade how bad a case is.

The team studied brain images from sixty-two HIV-positive patients treated in the era of strong HIV therapy. They report that the brain lesions seen on scans correlate with how severe the illness is. If scan patterns grade a case well, doctors could sort who needs the most urgent and intense care.
plos-pone-0002050:
Toru Nakamura and co-authors compared the pattern of behavior in mice and men, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Mental functions, and how psychiatric illness warps them, are hard to reach with molecular tools, since objective measures of behavior in animals were lacking. The team instead studied laws of behavioral organization, the math shape of how acts are timed.

As the title states, they report a universality in that organization across mice and humans, and its breakdown in illness. If the timing laws match, a mouse's act stream can stand in for aspects of human mental state that genes alone cannot show.
plos-pone-0002150:
Tal Arnon, Gal Markel, Ahuva Bar-Ilan, and co-authors explored a new way to aim the immune system at cancer, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Natural killer cells are immune cells that can kill tumor cells and infected cells. On their surface sit natural cytotoxicity receptors, including NKp46, NKp44, and NKp30, which help them pick out targets.

These receptors also exist in a loose, soluble form that floats free of the cell. The team worked on using those free forms to build new cancer immune therapies. If a receptor can be turned into a drug-like molecule, the killer cell's own targeting skill might be borrowed for treatment.
plos-pone-0002250:
Evelyne Derelle and co-authors described the life cycle and genome of a virus that infects a marine alga, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Large DNA viruses infect hosts from algae to humans and descend from an ancient common ancestor. In the oceans, algal viruses shape plankton blooms and steer the evolution of the tiny plants at the food web's base.

John George Hohman, a German immigrant healer in Pennsylvania, first published The Long-Lost Friend in 1820. This edition of 1850 carried his collection of charms and cures through German America. The book became the classic grimoire of Pennsylvania Dutch pow-wow, the folk healing tradition of that region.

Its pages give words to say over burns, bleeding, toothache, and sick cattle. Bible verses, short prayers, and folk recipes stand side by side. Pow-wow practitioners treated the book as a license and a toolbox in one. Families kept copies for daily use across generations. Everyday magic for farm and family is here in its most durable American form, still consulted today.
